newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr content to watch U.S. gyrations.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr content to watch U.S. gyrations.

text.p: The Australian dollar idled through a quiet day, content to watch the gyrations of the U.S. dollar as the market reacted to the G7's statement on foreign exchange values.
"It's probably been one of the most boring days in recent times," one Australian dollar trader lamented of a day that saw the dollar confined a narrow range just over US$0.7600.
"I think that's always the case when you get these movements on the big dollar," the trader said.
By 4.30 p.m. (0530 GMT) the dollar was at US$0.7598/08, from an an opening US$0.7599/04 and a Friday close of US$0.7605/10.
On the crosses, the Australian dollar ended at 93.28/38 yen and 1.2518/38, up from an opening 92.02/12 and 1.2459/74, but down on Friday's local close of 94.39/49 and 1.2721/36.
In trade weighted terms, the dollar closed at 58.1, a notch up on its opening but down on Friday's level of 58.3.
The main action was on the U.S. dollar, which while reflected in the ranges on the Australian dollar cross rates, in effect had little impact in the local unit.
The cause was the statement issued by the G7 which said: "We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected."

The initial reaction, based in the interpretation that the dollar's bull run had ended, saw the dollar sold heavily to lows of 120.30 yen and 163.50 marks, before it recovered as those who had missed earlier opportunities to buy the dollar appeared.

In the afternoon, the Japanese Ministry of Finance's Eisuke Sakakibara said a rate around 122.50 yen reflect the G7 agreement for currency market stability. In late trade, the U.S. dollar was at 122.70/75 yen and 1.6475/6480.
Traders said that with the market distracted, the widely expected Japanese selling of the Australian dollar related to maturing samurai bonds had failed to appear.

While some of that selling has been attributed to the three interest rate reductions that occurred in the second half of 1996, the odds on a fourth, which had been weighing on the dollar, appear to be lengthening.

The ANZ job advertisement series show a 3.3 percent rise in January, the second rise in the past three months and the largest rise for a year. In trend terms, the series was positive for the first time in two years.
Employment weakness was cited by the Reserve Bank as a key factor in the three rate cuts last year.

ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said while the data should be treated with caution due to volatility over the summer holiday period, given the rise in job ads and some strength in other indicators, "it does appear that the two year decline in the demand for labour may be coming to an end".
That said, if the Japanese appetite for sterling continues, even diminished chances of another rate cut may not provide support for the Australian dollar.
Key support for the Australian dollar was seen just above US$0.7585, with a break here opening the way for a move towards US$0.7500, analysts said.
If support held in the face of further selling, it was possible a base for a move to break higher could form.

"The factors which are driving the Australian dollar are really the intentions of Japanese investors -- whether they're still quite as attracted to Australian yields as they were or whether there are better opportunities in the sterling market, and the U.S. market," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
"A secondary issue is commodity prices which have stayed fairly weak, notably so the gold price," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
